verdict.rationale: Four authors describe the departure with concrete verbs of physical elevation parsed as passives of external agency: ἐπήρθη (aorist passive, Acts 1:9), ἀνεφέρετο (imperfect passive, Luke 24:51), ἀναλημφθεὶς and ἀνελήμφθη (aorist passive participle and indicative of ἀναλαμβάνω, Acts 1:11 and 1 Tim 3:16), each paired with εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. The subject is fixed as touchable flesh by Luke 24:39 (ψηλαφήσατέ με, σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα), and Acts 1:11 names the ascended one οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς and equates his going with his return by οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον. Heavy eyewitness vocabulary (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν, ἀτενίζοντες ἦσαν, ἐθεάσασθε) and the named place Bethany ground the scene spatially. The one polysemous foothold (ὑπολαμβάνω of the cloud, and the offer-up sense of ἀναφέρω elsewhere) is overridden by the surrounding passive-motion grammar and the locative phrases.

scripture.force: Just before the ascension scene the risen Jesus says ψηλαφήσατέ με (aorist imperative, handle me) and ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει (a spirit does not have flesh and bones). The lexical point is that the subject who is shortly lifted up is defined here as a touchable, flesh-and-bones body, not a disembodied spirit. This fixes the referent of the later motion verbs as a physical body.

Jesus leads them out (ἐξήγαγεν, aorist active) toward Bethany, lifts his hands (ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας, aorist active participle of ἐπαίρω), and blesses them. A named place, a bodily gesture, and an active personal subject set a concrete spatial scene, not a metaphor.

While he was blessing them he was parted from them (διέστη, aorist active of διΐστημι, a verb used elsewhere only of spatial or temporal separation) and was being carried up (ἀνεφέρετο, parsed 3IPI, imperfect passive of ἀναφέρω) into heaven (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The imperfect passive depicts ongoing elevation by an external agent, and the locative phrase gives a destination. ἀναφέρω is polysemous (it means offer up in Heb 7:27, 9:28, 13:15 and lead up a mountain in Matt 17:1, Mark 9:2), but εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν here selects the carry-up-to-heaven sense.

While they were watching (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν, genitive absolute, present participle) he was lifted up (ἐπήρθη, parsed 3API, aorist passive of ἐπαίρω) and a cloud (νεφέλη) took him (ὑπέλαβεν, aorist active of ὑπολαμβάνω) from their eyes (ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). The passive ἐπήρθη names external agency, the genitive absolute fixes eyewitness observation, and the departure point is visual. ὑπολαμβάνω is polysemous (suppose in Luke 7:43, Acts 2:15; take up in Luke 10:30), but the lift-up plus from-their-eyes context settles the physical sense.

They were gazing intently (ἀτενίζοντες ἦσαν, present participle plus imperfect of εἰμί, a periphrastic imperfect) into heaven (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν) as he was going (πορευομένου αὐτοῦ, genitive absolute, present middle participle). ἀτενίζω elsewhere always means fix the eyes on something visible (Acts 3:4, 7:55, Luke 4:20), so the verb plus the present participle of πορεύομαι reports a sustained, observed motion of a personal subject.

The two men call the ascended one οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὁ ἀναλημφθεὶς ἀφ ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν (ἀναλημφθεὶς parsed as aorist passive participle of ἀναλαμβάνω) and say οὕτως ἐλεύσεται (ἐλεύσεται parsed 3FMI, future of ἔρχομαι) ὃν τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε αὐτὸν πορευόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. The demonstrative οὗτος pins the referent to the same Jesus they watched, and οὕτως plus ὃν τρόπον equates the manner of departure with the manner of return, so a non-bodily reading of the departure would also empty the promised return.

The risen Jesus tells Mary μή μου ἅπτου (present middle imperative of ἅπτω, do not cling to me) οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα (ἀναβέβηκα parsed as perfect of ἀναβαίνω, I have not yet ascended). The same lemma ἀναβαίνω is predicated of the touchable body Mary tries to hold, linking the touchable subject to the not-yet-completed ascent.

Jesus forecasts τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀναβαίνοντα ὅπου ἦν τὸ πρότερον (present participle of ἀναβαίνω, the Son of Man ascending where he was before). The same ascent verb is applied to the Son of Man before the passion, so the later Luke and Acts narration uses an already-announced motion vocabulary, not a freshly invented metaphor.

Paul cites Ps 68:18 (the highest-voted cross-reference for this verse) and applies ἀναβὰς εἰς ὕψος (aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω, having gone up to a height) to Christ. ἀναβαίνω is the ordinary verb of physical going up across its 82 occurrences. αἰχμαλωτεύω is a true hapax (this verse only), so its precise nuance cannot be triangulated from canon usage, but the ascent verb itself is unambiguous.

Paul asks what τὸ ἀνέβη (aorist of ἀναβαίνω) implies εἰ μὴ ὅτι καὶ κατέβη (aorist of καταβαίνω) εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς. He pairs the standard up verb and down verb as a real spatial movement with a point of origin and a destination, which supports a literal reading of the ascent in v. 8.

The one who descended (ὁ καταβάς, aorist participle of καταβαίνω) is the same (αὐτός) who ascended (ὁ ἀναβάς, aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω) ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν (far above all the heavens). The locative ὑπεράνω plus the genitive plural assigns the ascended subject a real position, matching the Luke and Acts destination εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν.

The confessional hymn runs six aorist passives in a row (ἐφανερώθη, ἐδικαιώθη, ὤφθη, ἐκηρύχθη, ἐπιστεύθη, ἀνελήμφθη) with one relative subject. It opens ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί (was manifested in flesh) and closes ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ (was taken up in glory, parsed 3API, aorist passive of ἀναλαμβάνω, the same lemma as Acts 1:11). The σάρξ at the start and δόξα at the close keep the same fleshly subject in view through the taking up.

Luke opens the ascension narrative by saying the risen Jesus presented himself alive (παρέστησεν ἑαυτὸν ζῶντα, present participle of ζάω) δι ἡμερῶν τεσσεράκοντα, appearing to them (ὀπτανόμενος). The forty-day interval is set lexically by τεσσεράκοντα ἡμερῶν inside the same narrative unit that ends with the ascension in vv. 9 to 11, grounding the forty-day clause of the proposition.

complicating_texts.resolution: Jesus says οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς (ἀναβέβηκεν parsed as perfect of ἀναβαίνω). It uses the same ἀναβαίνω lemma as Eph 4:8 to 10 and is read of the Son who descended and would ascend. It limits who can ascend, the one originating from heaven, not whether a bodily ascent occurs, so it does not contradict the bodily lift in Luke and Acts.

A visionary or theological-motif reading could lean on the polysemy of ὑπολαμβάνω (the cloud took him), since the verb means suppose in Luke 7:43 and Acts 2:15. But the governing main verb is ἐπήρθη, the aorist passive of ἐπαίρω, which in its 19 occurrences always means a literal raising (eyes, hands, voice, sails), and it is bracketed by βλεπόντων αὐτῶν and ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν. The physical sense is therefore fixed by the surrounding grammar, not assumed.

The longer ending of Mark uses ἀνελήμφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν, lexically identical to Acts 1:11 and 1 Tim 3:16. Even though the longer ending is text-critically secondary, the verdict does not depend on it, since Luke 24 and Acts 1 stand independently.

variant_units_examined.note: A small group of witnesses omit καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. The clause is the majority reading. Even on the shorter text, διέστη ἀπ αὐτῶν plus the independent Acts 1:9 to 11 parallel preserves the bodily departure frame, so the verdict holds either way.
The reading ὅς versus θεός at the head of the hymn changes the grammatical subject of the relative chain but does not touch ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ, which is the load-bearing ascent clause.
The longer ending of Mark is text-critically disputed and is not required for the verdict, which rests on Luke 24 and Acts 1.

variants.note: All anchors lie outside the ingested ECM window (3 John 1.1 to 1.15), so no Coherence-Based Genealogical Method apparatus was examined. Variant readings are taken from the standard critical editions in shadow mode.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the passive motion verbs (ἐπήρθη, ἀνεφέρετο, ἀνελήμφθη), the locative εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, the eyewitness verbs, and the touchable σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα body as a single coherent report of a visible bodily relocation. This is the strongest reading on the surface lexical data.
Reads the ascent as the enthronement of the covenant mediator above all heavens (Eph 4:10), and the bodily lift is retained as the historical means of that enthronement.
Reads the ascent as the precondition for the present heavenly session and the future visible return promised in Acts 1:11, with the bodily ascent and bodily return held together by ὃν τρόπον.

Treats the ascent vocabulary as a cosmological or theological metaphor of exaltation rather than a spatial relocation, leaning on the polysemy of ὑπολαμβάνω and ἀναφέρω and on the cloud as a theophany symbol. Stated in its strongest form, it argues that upward language in an ancient three-tier cosmos need not assert literal travel. The lexical counterweight is that the governing verbs are passive verbs of physical raising bracketed by eyewitness verbs and a touchable body, which this reading must treat as figurative against the grain of their ordinary usage.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict is stable across the grammatico-historical, covenantal, and dispensational lenses. The visionary lens dissents, but it does so by reading the surface motion verbs and eyewitness framing figuratively rather than by deriving its reading from them.

stem_audit.notes: The stem states a concrete, testable event (a bodily ascent, a forty-day interval) without encoding a tradition-specific taxonomy, so the verdict is derived from the lexical data rather than smuggled by the wording. Occurrence counts and morphology in this file were verified by direct query of the lexical store (MorphGNT parsing and GreekLemma concordance) rather than taken from the capped input bundle.

lay_summary: The question is whether Christ ascended bodily into heaven forty days after his resurrection. Reading only the Greek text and standard lexical tools, the verbs across Luke, Acts, Ephesians, and First Timothy describe a physical event done to a physical subject. Just before the scene, Luke 24:39 has Jesus say handle me, a spirit does not have flesh and bones, so the one about to be lifted is a touchable body. Luke 24:51 then uses anephereto, an imperfect passive meaning he was being carried up, with into heaven. Acts 1:9 uses eperthe, an aorist passive meaning he was lifted up, and notes the disciples were watching and that a cloud took him from their eyes. Acts 1:10 piles on eyewitness words, they were gazing intently into heaven as he was going. Acts 1:11 names him this same Jesus and says he will come back in the same manner they saw him go, so treating the departure as mere symbol would also empty the promised return. Ephesians 4 pairs the ordinary up verb with the down verb to make a real spatial movement, and First Timothy 3:16 ends a chain of passives with he was taken up in glory, the same verb as Acts. The forty days is fixed by Acts 1:3. There are honest soft spots a careful reader should know. The cloud verb took him can elsewhere mean suppose, and the carried up verb can elsewhere mean offer up a sacrifice, so a few words are not decisive on their own. But the main verbs in each scene are passive verbs of physical raising, set beside watching eyes, a named place called Bethany, and a flesh-and-bones body. Across four authors the pattern is one consistent picture, and the variant readings (one clause missing in a few copies of Luke, the disputed longer ending of Mark, the who versus God reading in First Timothy) leave the verdict unchanged because Acts stands on its own.
